Static image export

Source: vignettes/static-export.qmd

save_image() writes a figure to PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG, PDF or EPS. It draws the figure with plotly.js’s own image export, using the plotly.js bundled with plotly.core, in a headless Chrome driven by the chromote package.

What’s new: no Python, no orca, and much faster

Static export in the plotly R package has needed software from outside R:

  • orca (orca(), now deprecated) needed the orca command-line utility, an Electron app installed separately with npm or a standalone installer.
  • Kaleido (save_image(), kaleido()) needed a Python installation set up for reticulate with the kaleido and plotly Python packages, and Kaleido 1.x also needs Chrome.

Getting a Python environment that reticulate finds, with the right packages in it, was the most common stumbling block.

plotly.core needs neither. Everything R needs is on CRAN: chromote (and rsvg, only for EPS). The one other thing, a browser, is found automatically, and if there is none chromote downloads one, after asking in an interactive session (see First-time setup).

orca Kaleido plotly.core
Installed with npm or a standalone installer Python, pip/reticulate::py_install() install.packages("chromote")
Python needed No Yes No
Browser Bundled (Electron) Chrome (Kaleido 1.x) Chrome, found or downloaded automatically
plotly.js used orca’s own Kaleido’s or plotly.core’s plotly.core’s, the same as the widget

It is also much faster. Kaleido 1.x, as the plotly R package calls it, starts a browser for every image; plotly.core starts Chrome once per R session and keeps it, so after the first image, exports take a fraction of a second:

Figure (700 × 500 PNG) Kaleido 1.5 (s) plotly.core (s) Faster
Scatter, 150 points 1.37 0.025 55×
Line, 100,000 points (scattergl) 2.81 0.27 10×
Heatmap, 500 × 500 1.86 0.49 3.8×
3D surface 2.35 0.59 4.0×
20 scatter figures, one after another 27.1 0.58 47×

Median of 5 exports each, after the first export of the session (which starts the browser: 1.3 s for plotly.core, 1.5 s for Kaleido), with the same figures and the same plotly.js (4.3.0); Kaleido 1.5.1 called through reticulate as kaleido.write_fig_sync() for each figure, as the plotly R package’s save_image() does. Measured on an Apple M3 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, Chrome 157, on 2026-11-16. The gain is largest for small figures, where starting the browser is most of Kaleido’s time, and for exporting many figures.

Saving an image 

fig <- px_scatter(
  px_data_iris(),
  x = ~sepal_width,
  y = ~sepal_length,
  color = ~species
)
png_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
save_image(fig, png_file, width = 700, height = 450, scale = 2)

The format is taken from the file extension:

Extension Format Notes
.png, .jpeg/.jpg, .webp Raster scale multiplies the resolution, e.g. scale = 2 for high-DPI screens
.svg Vector WebGL traces (scattergl, 3D, maps) are embedded as images
.pdf Vector The SVG image printed to a page the size of the figure
.eps Vector Converted from the SVG image; needs the rsvg package

width and height are in pixels. They default to the figure’s layout width and height, or 700 × 500.

LaTeX in titles and labels (see TeX()) is typeset with MathJax, which is loaded from a CDN the first time a figure needs it. Without internet access, the export still works but the LaTeX is left as plain text, with a warning.

Many figures

The first export starts Chrome, which takes a second or two. Later exports in the same R session reuse it and take a fraction of a second, so exporting many figures in a loop needs nothing special:

for (i in seq_along(figures)) {
  save_image(figures[[i]], sprintf("figure-%02d.png", i))
}

chrome_exporter() starts a browser of your own, to control when it starts and stops:

ex <- chrome_exporter()
ex$transform(fig, "figure.svg", width = 800, height = 500)
ex$shutdown()

First-time setup

Static export needs:

  • the chromote package, version 0.5.0 or later: install.packages("chromote")
  • a Chrome or Chromium browser (see below)
  • the rsvg package, only for EPS: install.packages("rsvg")

save_image() looks for a browser in this order:

  1. the browser set by the CHROMOTE_CHROME environment variable
  2. an installed Google Chrome or Chromium, found by chromote::find_chrome()
  3. a Chrome Headless Shell downloaded earlier by chromote

Most desktop machines with Chrome installed need no setup at all.

In an interactive session

When set-up is needed, an interactive R session asks once whether to run install_chrome(), which does all of it:

Static image export needs Chrome, which wasn't found. Run
plotly.core::install_chrome() to download Chrome Headless Shell (about 100 MB,
from Google's Chrome for Testing) and, on Linux, any shared libraries it
needs? Downloads are kept in your user cache for later sessions; no
administrator rights are needed. (Yes/no/cancel)

Answer yes and the export continues once the downloads are done. They are kept in your user cache, so later sessions and scripts on the same machine find them without asking. Answer no and save_image() stops with an error explaining the other options.

In a script, a scheduled job or CI

Rscript, scheduled jobs, CI runs and other non-interactive sessions never download anything on their own: without a browser, save_image() stops with an error. Set up a browser once, before the script runs, in one of these ways:

  • Run install_chrome() once, as the user the scripts run as. It does everything the interactive prompts would, without asking: it finds a browser or downloads Chrome Headless Shell, and on Linux downloads the shared libraries it lacks (see Linux servers). No administrator rights are needed.

    plotly.core::install_chrome()

  • Download Chrome Headless Shell with chromote, for example in a setup script or a Dockerfile:

    chromote::chrome_versions_add("latest-stable", "chrome-headless-shell")

    This is the same download the interactive prompt offers, kept in chromote’s cache for every later session of the same user.

  • Install Chrome or Chromium with the system’s package manager. chromote finds it in the usual locations.

  • Point CHROMOTE_CHROME at a browser that is installed somewhere else, for example in .Renviron:

    CHROMOTE_CHROME=/opt/chrome/chrome

To check what is available, chromote::find_chrome() shows the installed browser it would use, and chromote::chrome_versions_list("installed", "chrome-headless-shell") lists the shells already downloaded.

A script can check for a browser up front and fail early with a clear message:

if (is.null(tryCatch(chromote::find_chrome(), error = function(e) NULL)) &&
    !nrow(chromote::chrome_versions_list("installed", "chrome-headless-shell"))) {
  stop("No Chrome for static image export: run ",
       "chromote::chrome_versions_add('latest-stable', 'chrome-headless-shell') once")
}

Linux servers

A server without a browser usually lacks the shared libraries a browser needs, too, even after Chrome Headless Shell is downloaded: a desktop install of Chrome brings them in as dependencies, the download doesn’t. Before starting Chrome, plotly.core checks for them with ldd.

No administrator rights needed. On Debian, Ubuntu and RHEL-family systems (RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Fedora, Amazon Linux), plotly.core can get the missing libraries itself: it downloads the packages that provide them from the system’s own package repositories (apt-get download or dnf download, which any user can run), unpacks them into its cache (tools::R_user_dir("plotly.core", "cache")), along with the libraries those need in turn, and starts Chrome with them on its library path. Nothing is installed system-wide.

  • In an interactive session, save_image() asks first, as part of the same install_chrome() question when there is no browser yet, or on its own:

    Static image export needs shared libraries Chrome lacks (libgbm.so.1,
libxkbcommon.so.0). Run plotly.core::install_chrome() to download them from
your system's package repositories? Downloads are kept in your user cache
for later sessions; no administrator rights are needed. (Yes/no/cancel)

  • In a script, save_image() stops with the list of missing libraries and how to get them; run plotly.core::install_chrome() once to download them (and Chrome Headless Shell, if there is no browser).

This needs the system’s package lists, which servers normally have; slim container images often ship without them (refreshing them, apt-get update, needs root), and so do other distributions (SUSE, Arch, Alpine), where plotly.core instead shows the command to install the libraries.

With administrator rights, the libraries can be installed system-wide instead. When some are missing, the error shows the command for the system:

Chrome at /home/me/.cache/R/chromote/.../chrome-headless-shell can't start: shared libraries it needs are missing:
  libgbm.so.1, libxkbcommon.so.0
Download them into your user cache, without administrator rights, by running once:
  plotly.core::install_chrome()
Or install them with your system's package manager (this needs administrator rights):
  sudo apt-get install -y libgbm1 libxkbcommon0
Or install Google Chrome or Chromium, which brings them in.

The libraries a fresh server most often lacks are installed with:

# Debian, Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install -y libnss3 libnspr4 libatk1.0-0 libatk-bridge2.0-0 \
  libcups2 libdrm2 libgbm1 libxkbcommon0 libxcomposite1 libxdamage1 \
  libxfixes3 libxrandr2 libpango-1.0-0 libcairo2 libasound2

# RHEL, Rocky, AlmaLinux, Fedora, Amazon Linux
sudo dnf install -y nss nspr atk at-spi2-atk cups-libs libdrm mesa-libgbm \
  libxkbcommon libXcomposite libXdamage libXfixes libXrandr pango cairo \
  alsa-lib

Alternatively, installing the distribution’s Chromium package, or Google Chrome, installs the browser and everything it needs in one step; chromote then finds it, and no download is needed. On Alpine Linux, Chrome Headless Shell doesn’t run at all (it needs glibc): install Chromium (apk add chromium) and set CHROMOTE_CHROME=/usr/bin/chromium-browser.

When Chrome is found but still fails to start, the error shows what Chrome printed, with a hint for the common causes:

  • Running as root (common on servers and in containers): Chrome refuses to run as root with its sandbox. Allow it to run without:

    chromote::set_chrome_args(c(chromote::get_chrome_args(), "--no-sandbox"))

    chromote adds this flag itself inside Docker and on CI.

  • Too little shared memory (/dev/shm, small in some containers): add "--disable-dev-shm-usage" the same way.

Containers and CI

  • chromote adds the Chrome flags that containers and CI need (--no-sandbox, --disable-dev-shm-usage) when it detects them. Other flags can be added with chromote::set_chrome_args().
  • A minimal image needs the shared libraries listed under Linux servers; install them, or Chromium, in the image, along with Chrome Headless Shell (chromote::chrome_versions_add("latest-stable", "chrome-headless-shell")) so that nothing is downloaded when the container runs.
  • Text is drawn with the fonts Chrome can find. A minimal image may lack the figure’s fonts (plotly’s default is “Open Sans”, falling back to Verdana and Arial), which changes how text looks and is measured; install the fonts to match a desktop export.
  • WebGL traces are drawn with the GPU when there is one and in software (SwiftShader) otherwise, which works but is slower.

In R Markdown and Quarto

In documents rendered to formats other than HTML (PDF, Word, …), figures are included as images made by save_image(), when a browser is available. Rendering a document never offers to download one: without a browser, the figure is included as an HTML widget, as for HTML output, and a message points to this setup. The chunk option plotly.static = TRUE uses static images in HTML output too.

Troubleshooting

Message What to do
Static image export needs Chrome, which wasn’t found Set up a browser as described in First-time setup
Chrome … can’t start: shared libraries it needs are missing Run plotly.core::install_chrome(), or install them with the command shown (see Linux servers)
Chrome … failed to start Read Chrome’s output in the message; see Linux servers for running as root and shared memory
Static image export needs chromote 0.5.0 or later install.packages("chromote") (an older chromote can’t download Chrome Headless Shell)
EPS export needs the rsvg package install.packages("rsvg")
MathJax couldn’t be loaded …, so LaTeX is exported as plain text Check that the machine can reach cdn.jsdelivr.net
Unsupported image format Use one of the extensions in the table above

To remove what plotly.core has downloaded (the libraries, and with browser = TRUE Chrome Headless Shell), run remove_chrome().
